# Unifying the aminohexopyranose- and peptidyl-nucleoside antibiotics; implications for antibiotic design

**Authors:** Catherine M. Serrano; Hariprassada Reddy Kannareddy; Daniel Eiler; Michael Koch; Ben I. C. Tresco; Louis R. Barrows; Ryan T. Vanderlinden; Charles A. Testa; Paul R. Sebahar; Ryan E. Looper

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Chemistry, University of Utah, 315 S 1400 E, Salt Lake City, UT 84112 (USA) | bDepartment of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry, Yale University, 266 Whitney Ave., New Haven, CT 06250 (USA) | cDepartment of Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Utah, 30 South 1900 East, Salt Lake City, Utah, 84112 (USA) | dSynthetic and Medicinal Chemistry Core Facility, University of Utah, 315 S 1400 E, Salt Lake City, UT 84112 (USA)

## Abstract

In search of new anti-tuberculars compatible with anti-retroviral therapy we re-identified amicetin as a lead compound. Amicetin’s binding to the 70S ribosomal subunit of Thermus thermophilus (Tth) has been unambiguously determined by crystallography and reveals it to occupy the peptidyl transferase center P-site of the ribosome. The amicetin binding site overlaps significantly with that of the well-known protein synthesis inhibitor balsticidin S. Amicetin, however, is the first compound structurally characterized to bind to the P-site with demonstrated selectively for the inhibition of prokaryotic translation. The natural product-ribosome structure enabled the synthesis of simplified analogues that retained both potency and selectivity for the inhibition of prokaryotic translation.

## Abstract

Oldies but Goodies. Amicetin, first isolated in the 1950s is demonstrated to be the first prokaryotic-selective inhibitor of the ribosomal P-site. Simplification of amicetin’s structure provides compounds with comparable biochemical and whole-cell activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Given this selectivity, lack of cytotoxicity and dramatic structural changes that can be tolerated, amicetin holds promise as an anti-tubercular lead.

Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the world’s leading causes of death from a single infectious agent, second only to Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).1 TB-HIV co-infection is increasingly problematic and aggravated by the activation of hepatic cytochromes (CYP2C9 and CYP3A4) by current TB drugs (e.g. rifampin) that degrade Highly Active Anti-Retoviral Therapy (HAART) drugs.2 CYP induction renders plasma levels of the anti-retrovirals subtherapeutic, which accelerates the progression of TB due to weakened immune system.3 These drug-drug interactions also lessen the effectiveness of TB regimens compounding the emergence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) resistance.

There is a timely need for new TB therapeutics with global agencies defining the following criteria as their development goals: 1) potential to shorten and simplify duration of treatment; 2) effectiveness against multidrug-resistant strains; 3) compatibility with anti-retroviral therapy for TB-HIV co-infection; 4) ability to improve the treatment of latent infection; and 5) novel mechanism of action. 4,5 We launched a campaign to identify compounds that addressed these criteria. In doing so we identified the known natural product, amicetin, as an initial hit (Figure 1).6,7 We re-isolated amicetin to validate is activity.8 In our hands, this purified material demonstrated potent activity against Mtb H37Ra with an IC50 of 0.15 μg/mL (0.24 μM).9a It exhibited less than a 3-fold induction of CYP3A4 and CYP2A6 compared to rifampin which induces a 47- and 6-fold increase in these CYP mRNA levels, respectively.9b Considering the anti-mycobacterial activity and its lack of CYP induction we sought to study and utilize amicetin’s structural features to address the pressing clinical need for new TB therapeutics.

Amicetin, originally isolated from Streptomyces vinaceusdrappus, is a member of the broader family of aminohexopyranose nucleosides which includes the highly similar variants bamicetin, oxamicetin, SF2457 and cytimidine.10 The streptcytosines and cytosaminomycins represent more recent additions to this group.11 Blasticidin S12, gougerotin13, and TAN 1057A14 are peptidyl-nucleoside antibiotics that have been well appreciated to inhibit protein synthesis and characterized as binding to the ribosomal P-site.15,16 While amicetin was also appreciated to be an inhibitor of protein synthesis, the exact molecular underpinnings of its activity have remained elusive.17

Fox and Lichtenthaler hypothesized that the aminohexopyranose- and peptidyl-nucleoside antibiotics share a similar mechanism of action such that the α-methylserine fragment of amicetin would overlay with the guanidine unit in blasticidin S.18 This hypothesis would suggest that cytimidine, which retains the structural elements of blasticidin S should be active. In our hands however, as demonstrated below, cytimidine showed no activity at 100 μM against Mtb H37Ra.

Subsequently, the Mankin laboratory demonstrated that a single mutation confers amicetin resistance in H. halobium.19 This U2457C interchange has provided the speculative binding site of this antibiotic in the peptidyl transferase center (locating it near but not in the blasticidin S binding site). NMR experiments with a 35-mer RNA model of this site suggested that amicetin binds the ribosome in a highly strained conformation with an s-cis amide at the p-aminobenzoate-cytosine junction.20 Herein we demonstrate that amicetin does indeed bind the blasticidin S site but does so with the aminopyranose mimicking the guanidine of blasticidin S (not the α-methylserine) and binds in an extended (not folded) conformer.

Purified amicetin was co-crystallized with the 70S subunit of the ribosome of Thermus thermophilus (Tth) and the structure of this complex was solved at 3.5 Å resolution (Figure 2, PDB ID: 6CZR).21

The cytosine in amicetin forms a Watson-Crick base pairing of the cytosine motif and G2251(2262) [E. coli (Tth) numbering].15 The N,N-dimethyl-aminosugar forms a cation-π interaction with the nucleobase of A2439(2450). A2439(2450) is known to form a non-canonical wobble base pair with C2063(2052) in the native 70S ribosome.22 Disruption of this base pair by the cation-π interaction results in translational inhibition, and may account for the inhibitory properties of amicetin.23 Current resolution does not permit the discrete prediction of the rotamer of the α-methylserine fragment. However, the α-methylserine fragment is positioned between E80 of the ribosomal protein L16 and the phosphate of G2495(G2506)) of the 23S rRNA and likely makes electrostatic interactions between either or both.

As shown in Figure 3, there is striking overlap between the cytosine in amicetin and blasticidin S (PDB ID: 4V9Q) when bound to the Tth ribosome.18 Further, the positioning of the cationic amine (either the dimethylamine in amicetin or the guanidine in blasticidin S) is closely aligned to engage the cation-π interaction with A2439(2450) when bound to the Tth 70S subunit. The tether that connects the cytosine and the cationic amine spans a large cavity in the ribosomal P-site.

The fact that the disaccharide portion of amicetin makes very few contacts with the ribosome indicated that we could make two important strategic changes to the molecule: 1) we could remove the acid labile cytosine glycosidic linkage, for which hydrolysis produces cytimidine and cytosamine each of which are inactive and 2) the disaccharide could be synthetically simplified thereby increasing access to analogs.

To evaluate this hypothesis we targeted the simplified analogues 8–11 (Scheme 1). Nucleophilic aromatic substitution of sodium benzyloxide on pyrimidine 1, followed by acylation with 4-iodobenzoylchloride gave the pyrimidyliodobenzamide 2. Subsequent copper-catalyzed Buchwald amidation with α-methylserine derived carboxamide 3 gave masked cytimidine 4 which could be deprotected to provide cytimidine itself that was used for biological testing.24b

Careful hydrogenolysis of the benzyl group revealed the free cytosine that underwent selective alkylation at N-1 with propargyl bromide to give 5.25 Homologation of the pendant alkyne was accomplished via a three-component coupling with formaldehyde and either N,N-4-dimethylamino- or 4-N-Boc-amino-piperidine to give 6/7 respectively.26 Deprotection of 6 and 7 with methanolic HCl gave alkynyl analogues 8 and 9. Alternatively, hydrogenation followed by deprotection with methanolic HCl gave the saturated analogues 10/11.

Amicetin, blasticidin S and the analogues 8–11 were evaluated for their ability to inhibit Mtb growth, protein translation and proliferation of mammalian cells (Table 1). Amicetin was more potent than blasticidin S at inhibiting Mtb H37Ra (IC50 = 0.24 vs 19 μM). Conversely, blasticidin S is a significantly more potent inhibitor of in vitro translation measured using the E. coli S30 transcription/translation system (IC50 = 0.002 μM) than amicetin (IC50 = 0.207 μM). However, amicetin is very selective, inhibiting eukaryotic translation as measured in the rabbit reticulocyte lysate (RRL) system (Promega) with an IC50 = 20.3 μM and thus a selectivity index (SI) of 98. Blasticidin S retains significant potency against eukaryotic ribosomes (IC50 = 0.007 μM) representing a selectivity index of just 3.5. Amicetin displays significantly less toxicity to the Vero cell line (IC50 > 100 μM) vs blasticidin S (IC50 = 13.9 μM), likely reflecting this selectivity. Recently, the natural products bactobolin and actinobolin have also been demonstrated to bind in the P-site.27 They, like blasticidin S, are not selective inhibitors with equipotent inhibition of both prokaryotic and eukaryotic translation. These data reveal that amicetin represents the first compound structurally characterized to bind to the ribosomal P-site that inhibits prokaryotic translation with a meaningful level of selectivity. While the exact details underpinning this selectivity are unclear, it is likely that the p-aminobenzoate and α-methylserine units are critical. Studies to further understand this selectivity are currently ongoing.

When evaluating analogs 8–11, there was a striking structural dependence on both potency and selectivity. As demonstrated, potency tracked with flexibility of the linker and substitution of the amine with the saturated primary amine (11) being the most potent and only ~ 4-fold less potent than amicetin itself with an IC50 = 0.98 μM against Mtb-H37Ra. Interestingly the dimethylamino analog (10), which more closely resembles amicetin, was 10-fold less potent than 11. It is plausible that this increased potency results from a tighter cation-π interaction with the unsubstituted amine, or the formation of new hydrogen bonds with the rRNA phosphates that lie below the cation-π interaction.

The activities of 8-11 against Mtb H37Ra correlated to their ability to inhibit protein synthesis in vitro. Compound 11 (IC50 = 0.261 μM) is equipotent with amicetin (IC50 = 0.207 μM) at inhibiting E. coli translation while maintaining significant selectivity (111-fold) for inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. Correspondingly, 11 also displayed limited cytotoxicity with an IC50 > 100 μM against Vero cells. This comparable biochemical and cellular potency is striking given the simplification of the structure and the removal of 8 stereocenters.

Compound 11 was further examined in collaboration with the NIAID to evaluate promising anti-tubercular leads (Table 2). The compound was active against the virulent strain Mtb H37Rv (IC50 = 0.16 μM), under anaerobic conditions (IC50 = 0.54 μM) and intracellularly in THP-1 monocytes (IC50 = 6.7 μM). Given amicetin’s unique mechanism of action we were pleased to see that 11 demonstrated no cross-resistance, retaining activity against strains resistant to rifampicin (RIFR), isoniazid (INHR) and levofloxacin (FQR). Consistent with previous studies, amicetin[7] and 11 have activity limited to Mtb and some Gram-positive bacteria. We have recently completed a study detailing medicinal chemistry efforts to expand the spectrum of activity and these results will be published in due course.[28]

In conclusion, this study provides the first structural characterization of an inhibitor of the ribosomal P-site that selectively inhibits prokaryotic translation. Importantly, it demonstrates that amicetin shares significant overlap with the blasticidin S binding site and mimics the ε-N-methyl β-arginine with the dimethylamino group of the cytosamine sugar, not the α-methylserine substituent as previously thought. This example provides for a unified picture of how the aminohexopyranose- and peptidyl-nucleoside antibiotics inhibit translation. These results further demonstrate that amicetin can be synthetically minimized, to provide analogues that are more stable, retain potency and selectivity for inhibition of prokaryotic protein translation. Taken together this supports that the aminohexopyranose nucleoside antibiotics provide a tractable scaffold for the development of new anti-tubercular agents.
